title: University of Pennsylvania Team Demonstrates On-Chip Photonic Quantum Skyrmion Transfer in Nature Physics - Quantum Computing Report
author: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
text:
Schematic of on-chip photonic quantum skyrmion preparation and topology transfer from single photons to entangled states.

In a research paper published in Nature Physics, an international research team led by the University of Pennsylvania, in collaboration with the University of the Witwatersrand, Nanyang Technological University (NTU), and South China University of Technology, has demonstrated the preparation and reconfigurable transfer of photonic quantum skyrmions on an integrated nanophotonic chip.

By leveraging spin-orbit-locked microring resonators on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) platform, the researchers succeeded in transferring topological skyrmion structures from single photons to two-photon entangled states, establishing a noise-resilient quantum state transfer mechanism that maintains its topological invariant even after entanglement vanishes.

Photonic quantum skyrmions are topological light structures where the polarization (spin texture) across a beam profile wraps around every point on the Poincaré sphere an integer number of times. The topological invariant, known as the skyrmion number (Nsk), serves as a robust quantum observable.

The integrated nanophotonic circuit executes a three-stage topological protocol:

1. Path Entanglement Generation: Spontaneous four-wave mixing (SFWM) in tailored 650 nm wide silicon nitride spiral waveguides generates path-entangled photon pairs across distinct optical paths.2. Local Topology Encoding: Photon A passes through spin-orbit-locked microring resonators with asymmetric inner and outer sidewall gratings, coherently encoding a local single-photon skyrmion state with a skyrmion number of Nsk = 1.981 ± 0.002.3. Topology Transfer via BSM: An on-chip spin-momentum Bell state measurement (BSM) projects photon A onto the Bell basis, transferring the local single-photon skyrmion topology into a shared, non-local two-photon entangled skyrmion with a measured skyrmion number of Nsk = 1.981 ± 0.001.

Unlike conventional quantum teleportation, which fails immediately once the shared entanglement link breaks down, the skyrmion number exhibited resilience under depolarizing, phase-flip, and bit-phase-flip noise channels. Even when environmental noise reduced concurrence to zero, non-classical correlations (quantified by quantum discord) remained active, keeping the skyrmion number intact until extreme noise (γ ≈ 0.25) completely overwhelmed the system.

The study proves that quantum skyrmion numbers can act as topological witnesses for non-classical correlations, providing a blueprint for noise-tolerant quantum optical interconnects in distributed quantum computing networks.
